description: Based at Tokyo Metropolitan Tachikawa High School, Japan — open to students from around the world!
summary: Flame in Freefall is an SI-powered dashboard that makes NASA's microgravity combustion data easier to find, compare and trust for spacecraft and Moon-base fire safety. It brings together the 24 combustion investigations in NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) repository: what each one studied, its hardware, and the oxygen, air-flow and pressure conditions its tests recorded, set against the Moon-base atmosphere in the challenge brief (30% oxygen or more at 10.2 psi or less). Counting test by test, it finds that only one investigation, ACME CFI-G, ran tests at both levels together (20 of its 179 normal-flame tests), and that BASS, SAFFIRE-III, SAME and SAME-R record neither ambient oxygen nor pressure. A Fire Safety Insights page gives an SI-written reading of each record for preventing, detecting and suppressing fires; every statement cites numbered PSI passages, and statements whose numbers are not in their sources are removed automatically. The SAFFIRE Vision module checks the camera behind the SAFFIRE spacecraft fire experiments: it detects the distortion grid, measures how the lens bends it, and shows honestly that the published images are not enough to calibrate the camera.
details:
What it does. Flame in Freefall is an SI-powered dashboard that helps designers of spacecraft and Moon bases use NASA's microgravity combustion data. It answers three questions: which NASA fire experiments already ran at a Moon-base atmosphere, what each investigation means for preventing, detecting and suppressing fires, and how far the SAFFIRE camera images can be trusted for measurement.

  • Combustion Investigations: all 24 combustion investigations in NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) repository, filterable by the fire-safety area the challenge brief names (flammability, detection, suppression), hardware family and recorded conditions. Each has a page with its objective, approach, hypothesis, test-condition ranges, publications with DOI links and related investigations.
  • Moon-base coverage: counts the tests in NASA's experiment tables that ran at the brief's Moon-base atmosphere (30% oxygen or more, 10.2 psi or less). Only ACME CFI-G ran tests at both together: 20 of its 179 normal-flame tests. BASS, SAFFIRE-III, SAME and SAME-R record neither ambient oxygen nor pressure, so they cannot be placed against a Moon base yet.
  • Fire Safety Insights: an SI-written reading of each investigation for spacecraft fire safety. Every statement cites numbered passages from the PSI record, the test-condition ranges or the Moon-base counts. A script removes any statement that cites nothing, or uses a number its cited passages do not contain. The page says these are aims and methods, not measured burn results, and that the team has not yet reviewed them.
  • SAFFIRE Vision: image analysis of the SAFFIRE-1 distortion-grid images: preprocessing, checkerboard corner detection (231 corners, a 21 × 11 pattern), lens-bending measurement (row straightness RMS 8.05 px) and a calibration check, which shows the published images are not enough to calibrate the camera (one view per camera; 10 or more are needed).
  • Flame frames and reports: marks flame-coloured pixels in one uploaded still, and saves HTML/JSON reports of every run.

How it works. A Python FastAPI backend runs OpenCV on the grid images. A build script reads the downloaded PSI metadata and experiment tables; oxygen, flow and pressure columns are mapped by hand, converted to %, cm/s and psi, and each value names its source column. Oxygen in an inverse-flame burner stream is kept apart from the surrounding atmosphere. The insights are generated once with the Gemini API and checked automatically against their sources. The Next.js and TypeScript frontend shows it all, and labels anything that is SI-written, excluded or not NASA data.

Benefits and impact. Fire-safety researchers see in one place which experiments tested conditions close to a lunar habitat, and where the data runs out, with every number traceable to its NASA table. The gaps it finds point to the experiments still needed before a Moon base runs at higher oxygen and lower pressure.

Creativity and factors we considered. We chose to show what the data can and cannot support rather than invent results: unknown values are shown as "not recorded", not zero; SI text must cite its sources; and calibration stays blocked until there are enough views.

Tools. Python, FastAPI, OpenCV, NumPy, Pandas; Next.js 14, React 18, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Recharts; Google Gemini API; Playwright for testing; GitHub for collaboration.
